data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The nocturnal UHI is a coupled storage-and-trapping phenomenon, but the single best cross-city modulator is the ratio of urban impervious surface fraction to sky view factor (ISF / SVF), which captures both how much daytime heat is stored and how slowly it is released at night. Cities with high impervious cover and low sky view have the largest nocturnal gaps; cities with either low impervious cover or high sky view have smaller gaps.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If ISF / SVF does not correlate with nocturnal UHI gap across cities, the composite-modulator claim is falsified.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If either ISF or SVF alone correlates better than their ratio, the composite claim is unnecessary.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If anthropogenic heat or evapotranspiration explains more cross-city variance, the single-modulator claim is overturned.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Daytime: impervious surfaces store sensible heat proportional to their heat capacity and insolation. Night: the rate of cooling is governed by how efficiently the surface can lose heat radiatively, which is gated by SVF. The nocturnal gap is proportional to stored heat divided by cooling efficiency, which maps to ISF / SVF. This composite metric explains why two cities with the same thermal mass but different geometry, or the same geometry but different impervious fraction, have different gaps. It subsumes the separate claims of thermal mass and radiative trapping into a single dimensionless modulator.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
